subject: botany
question_text: Give examples for unicellular, colonial and filamentous algae.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section, Chapter 4 Plant Kingdom, book p.7, VSAQ 9. Only one source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand is physics-only and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card, not merely unrun. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Unicellular and colonial
steps.why: Algal body form ranges from one cell to a colony to a filament. Chlamydomonas is a single motile cell; Volvox is a colony of many such cells in one hollow ball.
common_mistakes: Writing Volvox as unicellular — it is a colony of many cells.
Misspelling Chlamydomonas — write the genus slowly; the name itself is marked.
steps.memory_tip: Size order C → V → S: Chlamydomonas (one cell), Volvox (colony ball), Spirogyra (thread).
steps.margin_note: One genus per body form; underline every genus name.

steps.label: Filamentous
lines: Cells joined end to end form a thread-
steps.why: In filamentous algae, cell division in one plane keeps the daughter cells attached in a row, giving a thread-like body. Spirogyra (the book's example) and Ulothrix are the standard genera.
common_mistakes: Writing Fucus or Laminaria here — they are large thalloid marine algae, not simple filaments.
steps.memory_tip: Spirogyra is the spiral thread — its spiral chloroplast runs along a filament.
steps.margin_note: One filamentous genus is enough; Spirogyra is the book's pick.

insider_note: Three named genera, one per body form, is the complete answer — a fourth example adds nothing to the marks.
